stem: A newborn girl has webbing between the third and fourth fingers with an extra digit (synpolydactyly). Sequencing shows an expanded polyalanine tract in HOXD13, a homeobox gene, and her father has milder hand findings.
oneliner: Newborn girl + synpolydactyly + expanded polyalanine tract in HOXD13 homeobox gene + father mildly affected → which type of protein?
ask: Which type of protein does the mutated gene encode?

options.B: Receptor tyrosine kinase for a growth factor
options.C: Structural collagen of the extracellular matrix

whyNot.B: Mutations (FGFR3) cause **achondroplasia**; HOX genes do not encode growth factor receptors
whyNot.C: Collagen defects give **brittle bone or joint laxity**, not digit patterning errors
whyNot.D: Connexin defects cause **deafness, neuropathy and skin disease**, not a segment-identity error
whyNot.E: Adhesion molecules matter for **tissue integrity**, not for setting limb position

why: **Homeobox (HOX) genes** encode **transcription factors** with a DNA-binding homeodomain. They set **segment identity along the anterior-posterior axis**, so mutations cause limb and axial malformations such as **synpolydactyly**.

idea.rule: HOX genes encode transcription factors that give each body segment its identity, so mutations cause limb and axial malformations.
also: 3' HOX genes are expressed earlier and more anteriorly than 5' genes (colinearity)
Sonic hedgehog (a signaling protein) patterns the limb anterior-posterior axis

stem: A 30-year-old healthy woman has normal development and a normal physical examination. A karyotype done for family screening shows a balanced paracentric inversion in one chromosome. She and her partner plan to start a family.
oneliner: 30F + healthy + normal exam + balanced paracentric inversion on karyotype + planning pregnancy → main problem?
ask: Which problem is she most likely to have?

whyNot.A: A balanced carrier has **no loss of genetic material**, so she herself is normal
whyNot.B: Associated with **X chromosome** abnormalities such as Turner syndrome, not an autosomal inversion
whyNot.C: A **Mullerian duct** malformation, unrelated to a chromosome inversion
whyNot.D: Arises from **disorders of sex development**; her normal examination excludes it

why: A balanced inversion carrier is **healthy**, but **crossing over within the inversion loop** gives gametes with duplications or deletions (and acentric or dicentric chromosomes). The result is **reduced fertility and miscarriages**.

idea.rule: Balanced carriers are normal themselves; their gametes are the problem.
also: Balanced Robertsonian translocation carriers: miscarriages or Down syndrome

stem: A 5-year-old boy has intellectual disability and mild dysmorphic features. His karyotype is normal. Microsatellite markers across the chromosome 15 region show that both of his alleles match his mother's two alleles at every marker there, and no allele from his father appears. Markers on other chromosomes show normal biparental inheritance, confirming paternity.
oneliner: 5M + intellectual disability + dysmorphism + normal karyotype + chromosome 15 markers: both alleles from mother, none from father; paternity confirmed → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism does the marker study show?

whyNot.A: Describes **earlier onset in later generations** through repeat expansion, not allele origin
whyNot.B: Shows **maternal transmission of mtDNA** and heteroplasmy, not nuclear chromosome 15 markers
whyNot.D: Needs **one allele from each parent** to be abnormal; here one parent contributes none
whyNot.E: Excluded: other markers show **biparental inheritance** and paternity is confirmed

answer: Uniparental disomy (both chromosome 15 copies from the mother)
why: Both copies of a chromosome from one parent is **uniparental disomy**. A normal karyotype can hide it, and with **imprinted genes** the missing parental contribution causes disease (Prader-Willi when both are maternal).

idea.rule: Uniparental disomy: both homologs from one parent, shown by markers, not karyotype.
also: Prader-Willi: maternal UPD 15 or paternal 15q11-13 deletion
Angelman: paternal UPD 15 or maternal deletion
Heterodisomy: two different homologs from one parent
Isodisomy: two identical copies of one homolog

stem: An 18-month-old girl has an unusually large tongue and tall, heavy build for her age. She has an abdominal wall defect repaired at birth and one side of her body larger than the other. An abdominal ultrasound finds a Wilms tumor, and genetic testing shows abnormal methylation at 11p15.
oneliner: 18-mo F + macroglossia + overgrowth + hemihyperplasia + prior abdominal wall defect + Wilms tumor + abnormal 11p15 methylation → which factor is excess?
ask: Overexpression of which growth factor best explains her overgrowth?

whyNot.A: Excess insulin explains the **neonatal hypoglycemia** of this syndrome, but the overgrowth comes from the imprinted IGF2 gene
whyNot.C: A **pituitary hormone** (excess gives acromegaly or gigantism) not an imprinting defect at 11p15
whyNot.D: Made in the liver **under growth hormone control**, not the imprinted 11p15 gene
whyNot.E: Drives **epithelial** growth through its receptor tyrosine kinase; its gene is not imprinted at 11p15

why: **Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome** results from abnormal **imprinting at 11p15**, giving **IGF2 overexpression** from the paternal allele. It causes **macroglossia, overgrowth, omphalocele** and a risk of **Wilms tumor** and hepatoblastoma.

idea.rule: Beckwith-Wiedemann: too much paternal IGF2 means overgrowth.
also: H19 and CDKN1C are maternally expressed at 11p15
Angelman: loss of maternal UBE3A at 15q11-13
